text: The Beginner project connected to one flat query result and built visuals directly on it. Nothing to relate, because there was only one table. This project is different on purpose: you import three separate objects, and let Power BI's relationship engine connect them.

Connect to AdventureWorks2012 with Get Data, SQL Server, and import all three staged views: vw_CarrawayWeeklySalesFact, renamed to Fact. vw_CarrawayProductDim, renamed to ProductDim. vw_CarrawayTerritoryDim, renamed to TerritoryDim. Renaming now, in Power Query, keeps every DAX measure in the next lesson readable.

Fact's OrderDate column is just a column, not a dimension. For DAX time intelligence, you need a real calendar table. Build one with CALENDAR, spanning the min to max OrderDate in Fact, then go to Model view and mark it as the official date table, pointed at the Date column. Skip that step, and time-intelligence measures silently compute wrong.

Then build three relationships in Model view: Fact's ProductID to ProductDim's ProductID, Fact's TerritoryID to TerritoryDim's TerritoryID, and Fact's OrderDate to Date's Date column. All three many-to-one, because many order lines share one product, one territory, or one date. All three single-direction, flowing from the dimension down to Fact — the standard star-schema setup.

Every measure in the next lesson, and every visual on both report pages after that, depends on these three relationships pointing the right way. Get the direction or cardinality wrong here, and no amount of correct DAX later fixes it. Next lesson: DAX measures with CALCULATE, a real step up from simple SUM and DISTINCTCOUNT.
